summary: Extends DHCP so the server can start a reconfiguration of a client that already has a lease, for example to give it a new address or new settings. Normally only the client starts these exchanges. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: DHCP hands out network settings such as an IP address. Usually the computer that needs settings asks for them. RFC 3203 lets the server push a change instead, by sending one message that tells the computer to renew now.

questions: how can a dhcp server push new settings to a client
subtitle: Lets a DHCP server tell one client to renew its lease now, instead of waiting for it to expire.

tldr.problem: In plain DHCP only the client starts an exchange, so a server cannot make a host pick up a new address or new settings before its lease runs out.
tldr.mechanism: The server sends a unicast FORCERENEW message, a new DHCP message type with the value 9. The client moves to the RENEW state and renews its lease the normal way, and a NAK can push it back to a full DISCOVER.
tldr.outcome: FORCERENEW MUST be authenticated with the DHCP authentication procedures, and flooding a client with bogus messages is a denial of service risk. RFC 6704 later updated this RFC.

facts.label: Delivery
facts.value: Unicast only; a multicast FORCERENEW is discarded

facts.label: Authentication
facts.value: MUST use the procedures in RFC 3118

facts.label: Retransmission
facts.value: Exponential backoff, limited number of attempts

today: RFC 3203 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2001 and is updated by RFC 6704. It has not been obsoleted, and it was written to be used together with the DHCP authentication procedures of RFC 3118.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The procedures in this document allow the dynamic reconfiguration of individual hosts. They extend DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) so that a DHCP server can trigger a reconfiguration of a single host, for example a new IP address and new local configuration parameters.

The extension works by introducing a unicast FORCERENEW message, which forces the client into the RENEW state. The document also describes the behaviour for hosts that use the DHCP INFORM message to obtain configuration information.

The document names two parties. The DHCP client is the host to be reconfigured using DHCP. The DHCP server is the server which configured that client.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP hands out network settings such as an IP address. Usually the computer that needs settings asks for them. RFC 3203 lets the server push a change instead, by sending one message that tells the computer to renew now.

sections.title: Force Renew Procedures
sections.content:
The DHCP server sends a unicast FORCERENEW message to the client. Upon receipt of it, the client changes its state to the RENEW state and then tries to renew its lease according to normal DHCP procedures.

If the server wants to assign a new IP address to the client, it replies to the DHCP REQUEST with a DHCP NAK. The client then goes back to the init state and broadcasts a DHCP DISCOVER message. The server can now assign a new IP address to the client by replying with a DHCP OFFER.

If the FORCERENEW message is lost, the server will not receive a DHCP REQUEST from the client, and it should retransmit the FORCERENEW message using an exponential backoff algorithm. Depending on the bandwidth of the network between server and client, the server should choose a delay. This delay grows exponentially as retransmissions fail. The amount of retransmissions should be limited.

The procedures assume a unicast FORCERENEW message. Receipt of a multicast FORCERENEW message by the client should be silently discarded.

A client may have obtained a network address through some other means, such as manual configuration, and used a DHCP INFORM request to obtain other local configuration parameters. Such clients should respond to a unicast FORCERENEW message with a new DHCP INFORM request, so as to obtain a potential new set of local configuration parameters. These procedures are limited to the set of options that are eligible for configuration by DHCP and should not override manually configured parameters.

The document also warns that using FORCERENEW to reconfigure a client address or local configuration parameters can lead to the interruption of active sessions, and that these procedures should therefore be used in controlled circumstances.

The rationale is given in the same section. The approach does not require new states to be added to the DHCP client implementation, which minimizes the amount of code to be changed. It also allows lease renewal to be driven by the server, which can be used to optimize network usage or DHCP server load.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends one unicast FORCERENEW message. The client moves to the RENEW state and renews its lease the usual way. If the server wants a different IP address, it answers the client's request with a NAK, and the client starts over with a DISCOVER. A client that gets a multicast FORCERENEW discards it without replying.

sections.title: Example Usage
sections.content:
The document gives three example situations.

In embedded DHCP clients, the autoconfiguration of home gateways, more generically network termination equipment, for public networking purposes can be achieved through means of DHCP. In order to allow service changes or service interruption, the FORCERENEW message can trigger the home gateway to contact the DHCP server prior to the expiry of the lease.

In a hospitality service scenario, a hotel-owned DHCP server can hand out limited-use IP addresses, which lets a customer consume local services or select external services from a web browser interface. In order to allow external services through other service providers, such as global internet services or enterprise VPN services, the DHCP server can trigger the client to ask for a new DHCP initialization session so as to obtain, for example, a globally routed IP address.

Under network renumbering, and under tightly controlled conditions, the FORCERENEW procedures can be used to brute force the renumbering of entire subnets, client per client, under control of a DHCP server.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives three uses for the new message. A home gateway can be told to contact the server before its lease ends. A hotel can move a guest from a local-only address to a globally reachable one. And an administrator can renumber a whole subnet one client at a time.

sections.title: The Extended DHCP State Diagram
sections.content:
The document redraws the DHCP client state diagram to show the new path. A new arrow runs from the Bound state to the Renew state, labelled DHCPFORCE, so a server can push a client that is already bound into a renewal before its lease runs down.

The rest of the diagram is the familiar DHCP flow. A combined "Init / Reboot" box sits at the top left. From it the client broadcasts a DISCOVER and enters Selecting, moves to Requesting after an OFFER and a broadcast REQUEST, and reaches Bound on an ACK. A client that is offered an address it must decline goes back to Init, and a NAK received in Init causes a restart. From Bound the client renews when T1 expires, rebinds when T2 expires, and a NAK after the lease has expired takes it back to Init with the network halted.
sections.plainLanguage: The client state diagram gains one arrow: a FORCERENEW message moves a client that already holds a lease straight into renewal. Everything else in the diagram is the usual DHCP path, from the first DISCOVER through binding, renewal and rebinding.

sections.title: Message Layout
sections.content:
The FORCERENEW message makes use of the normal DHCP message layout, with the introduction of a new DHCP message type. DHCP option 53, the DHCP message type option, is extended with a new value: DHCPFORCERENEW (9).

The IANA Considerations section records the same number: the new value for DHCP option 53 that indicates a DHCPFORCERENEW message is 9.
sections.plainLanguage: The new message reuses the ordinary DHCP message format. The only change is a new value, 9, added to the DHCP message type option, which is option 53.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document notes that in some network environments FORCERENEW can be used to snoop and spoof traffic. The FORCERENEW message MUST be authenticated using the procedures described in the DHCP authentication document, RFC 3118. FORCERENEW messages failing the authentication should be silently discarded by the client.

The mechanism described in the document is vulnerable to a denial of service attack through flooding a client with bogus FORCERENEW messages. The calculations involved in authenticating the bogus FORCERENEW messages may overwhelm the device on which the client is running.
sections.plainLanguage: A FORCERENEW message must be authenticated, using the method in RFC 3118, and a client should quietly drop any message that fails the check. A flood of forged FORCERENEW messages is a denial of service risk, because checking each one can overload the client.

messages.label: FORCERENEW
messages.note: Unicast message that moves the client into the RENEW state.

messages.label: DHCPREQUEST
messages.note: The client renews its lease the normal way.

messages.label: DHCPNAK
messages.note: Sent when the server wants to assign a new IP address.

messages.label: DHCPDISCOVER
messages.note: The client goes back to the init state and broadcasts.

messages.label: DHCPOFFER
messages.note: The server assigns a new IP address.
